title: The percentage of people testing positive has decreased in England, Wales, Northern Ireland and Scotland
subtitle: Official estimates of the percentage of the population in England, Wales, Northern Ireland and Scotland testing positive for the coronavirus (COVID-19) on nose and throat swabs, from 3 May 2020
commentary: The percentage of people testing positive for the coronavirus (COVID-19) decreased in all four UK countries in the week ending 6 February 2021. In England, it is estimated that around 1 in 80 people (695,400 people) in the community population had COVID-19. It is estimated that 1 in 85 in Wales (35,300 people), 1 in 75 in Northern Ireland (24,400 people) and 1 in 150 (35,400 people) in Scotland were infected.
sourcename: Coronavirus (COVID-19) Infection Survey

title: The percentage of people testing positive has fallen in most regions in England
subtitle: Estimated percentage of the population testing positive for the coronavirus (COVID-19) on nose and throat swabs, daily, by region, since 27 December 2020, England
commentary: The percentage of people testing positive has decreased in all regions in England in the most recent week (ending 6 February 2021), except for in the South West where the rate appears to have levelled off. Despite rates falling in London, it still has the highest positivity rate of all regions.
sourcename: Coronavirus (COVID-19) Infection Survey

title: London has the highest COVID-19 positivity rate
subtitle: Estimated percentage of the population testing positive for the coronavirus (COVID-19) on nose and throat swabs, by sub-regional geography, England, from modelling the most recent six days of data, 31 January to 6 February 2021
commentary: In the week ending 6 February 2021, the highest positivity rates were seen in London, followed by the West Midlands. The South East and South West had the lowest percentages of people testing positive for COVID-19.
sourcename: Coronavirus (COVID-19) Infection Survey

title: Cases compatible with the new UK variant decreased in England, Wales and Northern Ireland
subtitle: Positivity rates for cases that are compatible with the new variant of the coronavirus (COVID-19), not compatible with the new UK variant, and where the virus was too low for the variant to be identifiable, on nose and throat swabs, by country, daily, since 27 December 2020, England, Wales, Northern Ireland and Scotland
commentary: In England, Wales and Northern Ireland, the positivity rate for cases compatible with the new UK variant of COVID-19 decreased. Rates of new UK variant compatible cases appear to have levelled off in Scotland. Caution should be taken when interpreting trends in Wales, Northern Ireland and Scotland because of wide credible intervals and relatively small sample sizes.
sourcename: Coronavirus (COVID-19) Infection Survey

title: Cases compatible with the new UK variant have fallen in most regions in England
subtitle: Positivity rates for cases that are compatible with the new variant of the coronavirus (COVID-19), not compatible with the new variant, and where the virus was too low for the variant to be identifiable, on nose and throat swabs, by region, daily, since 27 December 2020, England
commentary: Positivity rates for cases compatible with the new UK variant of COVID-19 increased sharply in December 2020.  In the week ending 6 February 2021, cases compatible with the new UK variant decreased in all regions except Yorkshire and The Humber, the East Midlands, and the South West where the trend is uncertain.
sourcename: Coronavirus (COVID-19) Infection Survey

title: The percentage of people testing positive for COVID-19 has decreased in all age groups
subtitle: Estimated percentage of the population testing positive for the coronavirus (COVID-19) on nose and throat swabs, daily, by age group, since 27 December 2020, England
commentary: The percentage of people testing positive for COVID-19 decreased in all age groups in the most recent week (ending 6 February 2021). Adults aged 35 to 49 years had the highest proportion testing positive (1.24%), while adults aged 70 years and over continued to have the lowest (0.74%).
sourcename: Coronavirus (COVID-19) Infection Survey

title: The most commonly reported symptoms among people testing positive were cough, fatigue and headache
subtitle: Percentage of people with symptoms, including only those who have a strong positive test (cycle threshold (Ct) less than 30), from 1 October 2020 to 30 January 2021, UK countries
commentary: Cough, fatigue and headache were the most common symptoms reported in positive COVID-19 cases across the four UK countries. Abdominal pain, diarrhoea and nausea were less commonly reported. Similar trends in reported symptoms can be seen in all four UK countries.
sourcename: Coronavirus (COVID-19) Infection Survey: characteristics of people testing positive for COVID-19, countries of the UK

title: Coronavirus (COVID-19) Infection Survey and Real-time Assessment of Community Transmission study show similar trends over time
subtitle: Estimated percentage of the community population testing positive for the coronavirus (COVID-19), 27 April 2020 to 6 February 2021, England
commentary: The Coronavirus (COVID-19) Infection Survey (CIS) estimated that 1.28% of people in England had COVID-19 in the week ending 6 February 2021. The latest data from the Real-time Assessment of Community Transmission (REACT) study estimated 1.57% of the population to be infected between 6 and 22 January 2021. REACT and CIS show similar trends over time, with positivity rates much higher than in the beginning of December 2020. CIS and REACT both estimate how many infections there are in the community, although they use different methods and publish data at different times.
sourcename: Coronavirus (COVID-19) Infection Survey and Real-time Assessment of Community Transmission (REACT) study

title: The number of registered deaths was 40.8% above the five-year average in the latest week
subtitle: Number of deaths registered by week, England and Wales, 28 December 2019 to 5 February 2021
commentary: The total number of deaths registered between 7 March 2020 and 5 February 2021 in England and Wales was 586,964. Of these deaths, 119,147 mentioned the coronavirus (COVID-19) on the death certificate, equal to 20.3% of all deaths in England and Wales. In the latest week, deaths from all causes were 40.8% above the five-year average, but of those, the number of deaths not involving COVID-19 was below average.
sourcename: Deaths registered weekly in England and Wales, provisional

title: Deaths involving COVID-19 decreased by 13.2% compared with the previous week
subtitle: Deaths involving and due to the coronavirus (COVID-19), and influenza and pneumonia, deaths registered in 2020 and 2021, England and Wales
commentary: In the week ending 5 February 2021, the number of deaths involving the coronavirus (COVID-19) registered in England and Wales decreased by 13.2% compared with the previous week, to 7,320. This accounted for nearly half (42.6%) of all deaths registered that week. Coronavirus was the underlying cause of death for 89.1% of deaths involving COVID-19. In contrast, only 6.1% of deaths involving influenza or pneumonia had these conditions listed as the underlying cause of death.
sourcename: Deaths registered weekly in England and Wales, provisional

title: The number of deaths in the latest week was higher than the five-year average in all English regions and Wales
subtitle: Number of deaths in Wales and regions in England, registered between 28 December 2019 and 5 February 2021
commentary: The number of deaths involving the coronavirus (COVID-19) decreased in all English regions in the latest week. This is the first time a decrease has been reported in all regions since week ending 10 July 2020. However, the total number of deaths registered was higher than the five-year average in all English regions and Wales for the 13th week in a row. The largest increase on the five-year average was seen in London, where total deaths were 69.8% higher than expected.
sourcename: Deaths registered weekly in England and Wales, provisional

title: Nearly three-quarters of deaths involving COVID-19 were in people aged 75 years and over in the latest week
subtitle: Number of deaths registered by week and age group, 28 December 2019 to 5 February 2021, England and Wales
commentary: Throughout the pandemic, most deaths have been seen in older age groups. In the week ending 5 February 2021, nearly three-quarters of deaths involving the coronavirus (COVID-19) in England and Wales were in people aged 75 years and over. The number of deaths involving COVID-19 decreased in just over half of the age groups, with the biggest decrease seen in those aged 90 years and over compared with the week before (298 fewer deaths).
sourcename: Deaths registered weekly in England and Wales, provisional

title: Excess deaths were above the five-year average in private homes, hospitals and care homes
subtitle: Number of excess deaths by place of occurrence, registered between 7 March 2020 and 5 February 2021, England and Wales
commentary: The number of deaths involving the coronavirus (COVID-19) decreased in hospitals, private homes, care homes, other communal establishments and elsewhere, but increased in hospices in the week ending 5 February 2021. Deaths involving COVID-19 accounted for 58.0% of all deaths in hospitals, compared with 61.9% in the week before. In care homes this proportion decreased to 45.5% from 49.0% in the previous week.
sourcename: Deaths registered weekly in England and Wales, provisional

title: Caring, leisure and other service occupations saw high COVID-19 death rates
subtitle: Age-standardised mortality rates of death involving the coronavirus (COVID-19) in England and Wales, by major occupational group, deaths registered between 9 March and 28 December 2020
commentary: Between 9 March and 28 December 2020, there were 7,961 deaths involving COVID-19 in the working age population (those aged 20 to 64 years). Almost two-thirds of these deaths (64.4%) were among men, compared with 35.6% among women. Men working in caring, leisure and other services, and elementary occupations had the highest rates of deaths with COVID-19. For women, occupations with the highest rates were process, plant and machine operatives, and caring, leisure and other services.
sourcename: Coronavirus related deaths by occupation

title: COVID-19 mortality risk for most disabled groups is higher than non-disabled groups, although the risk is substantially reduced after adjusting for other characteristics
subtitle: Hazard ratios for death involving COVID-19 for disabled men and women relative to non-disabled people of the same sex, adjusting for age, residence type, geography, socio-economic and demographic factors, and comorbidities, England: 24 January to 20 November 2020
commentary: After adjusting for a range of factors, compared with non-disabled people, an increased risk of death involving COVID-19 remained for more-disabled and less-disabled women (1.4 and 1.2 times respectively) and more-disabled men (1.1 times) but not for less-disabled men. Disability status was defined according to the 2011 Census, with more-disabled and less-disabled referring to people who reported their daily activities as "limited a lot" or "limited a little", respectively.
sourcename: Updated estimates of coronavirus (COVID-19) related deaths by disability status, England: 24 January to 20 November 2020

title: COVID-19 mortality risk for people with a learning disability is higher than for people with no learning disability, although risk is substantially reduced after adjusting for other characteristics
subtitle: Hazard ratios for death involving COVID-19 for men and women with a learning disability relative to people with no learning disability of the same sex, adjusting for age, residence type, geography, socio-economic and demographic factors, and comorbidities, England: 24 January to 20 November 2020
commentary: After adjusting for a range of factors, people with a diagnosed learning disability remained at greater risk (1.7 times) of COVID-19 mortality than with those with no learning disability.
sourcename: Updated estimates of coronavirus (COVID-19) related deaths by disability status, England: 24 January to 20 November 2020

title: Compliance with preventative measures remains high
subtitle: Great Britain, 27 January to 7 February 2021
commentary: There are several measures in place to help curb the spread of the coronavirus (COVID-19), such as handwashing, use of face coverings, avoiding physical contact and self-isolating. Compliance with most measures remained high this week (3 to 7 February 2021), with 90% of adults reporting always or often handwashing after returning home, 95% using a face covering and 93% avoiding physical contact when outside their home. Around 9 in 10 (90%) adults reported always or often maintaining social distance when meeting up with other people outside their support bubble.
sourcename: Coronavirus and the social impacts on Great Britain

title: Personal well-being remains at some of the lowest levels since the survey began in March 2020
subtitle: Great Britain, March 2020 to February 2021
commentary: Personal well-being scores for life satisfaction (6.4), happiness (6.5) and feeling that the things done in life are worthwhile (7.1) remained at some of the lowest levels recorded since the survey began in March 2020. The anxiety score (4.2) has improved compared with early January 2021 (4.6), when the highest score since April 2020 was reported.
sourcename: Coronavirus and the social impacts on Great Britain

title: The proportion of adults who felt that it will take more than a year for life to return to normal fell slightly
subtitle: Great Britain, March 2020 to February 2021
commentary: The proportion of adults who felt that it will take more than a year for life to return to normal fell slightly to around 1 in 4 (27%), but remains higher than the proportion who feel life will return to normal in six months or less (21%).
sourcename: Coronavirus and the social impacts on Great Britain

title: People aged 70 years and over are more likely to have had or to accept the vaccine than younger adults
subtitle: Proportion of adults reporting they had received the COVID-19 vaccine or would be likely to have the vaccine if offered, by age, Great Britain, 3 to 7 February 2021
commentary: Over 9 in 10 (92%) adults reported that they had either received the COVID-19 vaccine or are likely to have the vaccine if offered. This includes adults who have accepted and are waiting to receive it. This proportion increased with age, from 83% of those aged between 16 and 29 years to 99% of those aged 70 years and over.
sourcename: Coronavirus and the social impacts on Great Britain

title: Around 3 in 4 adults would get a COVID-19 test as part of mass testing even if they had no symptoms
subtitle: Great Britain, 3 to 7 February 2021
commentary: If mass testing were available in their area, around 3 in 4 (74%) adults said they would be likely to get a test, even if they had no symptoms. This is an increase compared with last week (69%, week ending 27 to 31 January 2021) and is the highest proportion recorded. This proportion was lower amongst younger age groups, ranging from 64% of those aged 16 to 29 years compared with 78% of those aged 50 to 69 years.
sourcename: Coronavirus and the social impacts on Great Britain

title: In recent weeks, the proportion of adults staying at home or only leaving for essential needs remains higher than during the winter 2020 restrictions
subtitle: Percentage of adults that reported staying at home or only leaving for work, exercise, essential shopping or medical needs and daily road traffic index, Great Britain, May 2020 to February 2021
commentary: Despite recent decreases, the proportion of adults reporting staying at home or only leaving for work, exercise, essential shopping or medical needs (56%, 3 to 7 February 2021) remains higher than during the winter 2020 restrictions (prior to the early 2021 lockdown). The volume of car traffic was reduced to a similar level in the early 2021 lockdown (51% of the level observed in the first week of February 2020) as seen in the spring 2020 lockdown (51% between 14 and 17 May 2020).
sourcename: Coronavirus and the social impact on Great Britain: Exploring behaviours during the different lockdown periods

title: Most minority ethnicities have higher COVID-19 mortality rates
subtitle: Rate of death involving coronavirus (COVID-19) by ethnic group and sex relative to the white population, England, 2 March to 28 July 2020
commentary: Death rates for most ethnic minorities are higher compared with White ethnic groups. After accounting for where people live and social and economic factors (including people’s jobs, education and housing conditions), the gap lessens but is still significant.
sourcename: Updating ethnic contrasts in deaths involving the coronavirus (COVID-19), England and Wales

title: Individuals from the "Other" ethnic group had significantly greater positivity rates in the North West, Yorkshire and The Humber, East Midlands, West Midlands, and the South East
subtitle: The odds ratios of individuals in the "Other" ethnic group testing positive for coronavirus (COVID-19) on a swab test compared with individuals from the White ethnic group by region, England, between 4 October and 28 November 2020
commentary: Individuals from the "Other" ethnic group were more likely to test positive for the coronavirus (COVID-19) compared with those from the "White" ethnic group in the North West, Yorkshire and The Humber, East Midlands, West Midlands, and the South East.  There was no evidence supporting a lower risk of testing positive in those from the "Other" ethnic group in any region. After adjusting for differential effects of ethnicity by region, there was no evidence that the effect of ethnicity varied over time or by age.
sourcename: Coronavirus (COVID-19) Infection Survey: characteristics of people testing positive for COVID-19 in England

title: Some ethnic groups are more likely to work in jobs with higher COVID-19 death rates
subtitle: Proportion of ethnic group within occupations and COVID-19 death rate, England and Wales, deaths involving COVID-19 registered between 9 March and 25 May 2020
commentary: Black and Asian men are more likely to work in occupations that have had a higher risk of death involving COVID-19, such as transport, security and cleaning. For working women, there were higher rates of death involving COVID-19 in four professions including nursing, and people working as care workers or home carers. Of women working as care workers and home carers, a relatively high proportion were from Black ethnic backgrounds (13.2%). There were also higher proportions of women in nursing from Indian, Black and Other ethnic backgrounds.
sourcename: Coronavirus (COVID-19) related deaths by occupation, England and Wales

title: Multi-generational households with someone aged 70 years and older are more common for people of Bangladeshi or Pakistani ethnicity
subtitle: Proportion of households with at least one person aged 70 years or over by ethnic group of that person, by mix of ages in the household, UK, 2018
commentary: During the first national lockdown, people in the more vulnerable, older age groups were asked to shield and minimise contact with other people to reduce their risk of infection. Older people living in larger households may have found it more difficult to shield practically. Multi-generational households are much more common among ethnic minority groups, particularly those in the Pakistani, Bangladeshi or Indian ethnic groups.
sourcename: Coronavirus (COVID-19) roundup

title: People from minority ethnic groups are less likely to have access to a private garden
subtitle: Percentage of people with access to a private garden, by ethnic group, England, 2014 to 2019
commentary: During lockdown, many people found solace in a garden or outdoor space. In England, those in the Black ethnic group are nearly four times as likely as people in the White ethnic group to have no outdoor space at home (37% compared with 10%) – that is no private or shared garden, a patio or a balcony. After accounting for urban and rural living, age, social class, and whether they had children, the statistics remained significantly different.
sourcename: One in eight British households has no garden

title: Most ethnicity groups reported worse mental health during the pandemic
subtitle: Fully adjusted average change in GHQ-12 scores of those aged 16 years and over between 2019 and April 2020 by ethnic group, UK, 2019 and April 2020
commentary: Over a third (36%) of those from the Indian ethnic group reported increased or persistent loss of sleep over worry, compared with less than a quarter (23%) of White British respondents and 18% of those in the Other White ethnic groups. Around a third of those from the Black, African, Caribbean or Black British ethnic group (35%) also reported this.
sourcename: Coronavirus and the social impacts on different ethnic groups in the UK: 2020

title: COVID-19 was the leading cause of death in December 2020 in England
subtitle: Age-standardised mortality rate for selected leading causes of death, per 100,000 people, England, deaths registered in December 2020
commentary: Coronavirus (COVID-19) was the leading cause of death in December 2020, with 233.6 deaths per 100,000 people in England (10,973 deaths). This was the second consecutive month where COVID-19 was the leading cause of death. In December 2020, 6 of the 10 leading causes of death were significantly lower than the five-year average (2015 to 2019), with only the signs, symptoms, and ill-defined conditions, influenza and pneumonia, and malignant neoplasm of prostate categories having similar mortality rates to the five-year average. In 2020, based on provisional data, the leading cause of death in England was COVID-19, accounting for 12.1% of all deaths.
sourcename: Monthly mortality analysis, England and Wales

title: Deaths due to COVID-19 in each Middle layer Super Output Area in England and Wales
subtitle: Number of deaths due to COVID-19 in Middle layer Super Output Areas, England and Wales, deaths registered between 1 March and 31 December 2020
commentary: The interactive map allows you to see the cumulative number of monthly deaths due to COVID-19 in each area. Points on the map are placed at the centre of the local area they represent and do not show the actual location of deaths. The size of the circle is proportional to the number of deaths. Deaths “due to COVID-19” include only deaths where COVID-19 was the underlying cause of death.
sourcename: Monthly mortality analysis, England and Wales

title: COVID-19 positivity rates in secondary and primary schools
subtitle: Estimates of positive test results for COVID-19 in schools
commentary: Among people attending school on the day of testing, 1.24% (95% confidence interval: 0.96% to 1.58%) of pupils (65 out of 5,235 tested) and 1.29% (95% confidence interval: 0.96% to 1.68%) of staff (53 out of 4,122 tested) tested positive for current infection of COVID-19. The differences between positivity rates in primary and secondary schools are not statistically significant.
sourcename: COVID-19 Schools Infection Survey Round 1, England: November 2020

title: COVID-19 positivity rates in secondary and primary schools by virus prevalence
subtitle: Estimates of positive test results for COVID-19 in schools by virus prevalence
commentary: Among people attending school on the day of testing, similar proportions of staff and pupils tested positive for COVID-19 when comparing school type (that is, primary pupils and primary staff) within areas with similar level of virus prevalence. For example, in secondary schools in high prevalence areas, 1.73% of pupils (95% confidence interval: 1.18% to 2.43%) and 1.62% of school staff (95% confidence interval: 1.12% to 2.27%) tested positive for current infection. The differences between school type and virus prevalence are not statistically significant.
sourcename: COVID-19 Schools Infection Survey Round 1, England: November 2020

title: Hospital admissions involving COVID-19 decreased but remain high
subtitle: Overall COVID-19 positive hospital admission rates per 100,000, England, weeks ending 9 August 2020 to 7 February 2021
commentary: In the week ending 7 February 2021, confirmed coronavirus (COVID-19) hospital admission rates in England decreased to 19 per 100,000 people. This is almost half the rate seen in the week ending 17 January 2021 (36 per 100,000 people).
sourcename: Coronavirus (COVID-19) weekly insights: latest health indicators in England

title: Hospital admissions involving COVID-19 decreased in all regions in England, but deaths increased in most regions
subtitle: Change in hospital admission rates and numbers of deaths involving COVID-19 from previous week, England, weeks ending 7 February and 29 January 2021
commentary: In the week ending 7 February 2021, confirmed coronavirus (COVID-19) hospital admission rates decreased in all regions in England, with the largest fall recorded in the West Midlands. However, the West Midlands continued to have the highest hospital admission rate of all regions, at 26.7 per 100,000 people. The number of registered deaths involving COVID-19 increased in most regions in England, with the largest increase seen in the South West (week ending 29 January).
sourcename: Coronavirus (COVID-19) weekly insights: latest health indicators in England

title: The majority of COVID-19 infections are in young people, but hospital admissions and deaths are more common in older age groups
subtitle: Estimated percentage of the population testing positive for COVID-19 in the week ending 6 February 2021, hospital admission rates in the week ending 7 February 2021, and deaths registered in the week ending 29 January 2021, by age, England
commentary: Adults aged 35 to 49 years were most likely to test positive for COVID-19 in the week ending 6 February 2021. While positivity rates were lowest in adults aged 70 years and over, most deaths and hospital admissions involving COVID-19 were seen in people aged 85 years and over. Children aged 5 to 14 years remained the group least likely to be hospitalised with COVID-19. Almost 90% of deaths involving COVID-19 to date are among people aged 65 years and over.
sourcename: Coronavirus (COVID-19) weekly insights: latest health indicators in England

title: Most students’ mental health has worsened as a result of the pandemic
subtitle: Responses from students to "how has the coronavirus impacted your mental health?", UK, 2020
commentary: According to a survey of university students in 2020, 57% reported their mental health was either a little worse (43%) or much worse (15%) because of the coronavirus pandemic. Over a quarter (28%) said their mental health was the same, and 15% said their mental health was either a little better or much better since the pandemic. Findings from a variety of studies looking at student behaviours and wellbeing, including the ONS’s Student COVID-19 Insights Survey, have been presented in Coronavirus and the impact on students in higher education in England: September to December 2020.
sourcename: Coronavirus and the impact on students in higher education in England: September to December 2020

title: Fewer students report high well-being compared with others aged 20 to 24 years
subtitle: Personal well-being measures scoring “very high” for full-time undergraduate students and for young people aged 20 to 24 years, UK, 2016 to 2020
commentary: Prior to the coronavirus pandemic, student well-being had been decreasing over the last four years, according to data from the Student Academic Experience Survey. On four main measures of personal well-being (life satisfaction, feelings that things done in life are worthwhile, happiness, low anxiety), undergraduate students report substantially lower levels of well-being compared with the general population aged 20 to 24 years. However, different collection methods used in the surveys completed by students and the wider population could contribute to this difference.
sourcename: Coronavirus and the impact on students in higher education in England: September to December 2021

title: COVID-19 cases among students at Exeter university rose sharply following the start of term
subtitle: All cases among students by day, and NHS testing cases by day for those aged over 21 years in Exeter, 2 September 2020 to 16 November 2020
commentary: Data from Exeter University showed a high number of COVID-19 cases among students in the city following the start of term in September 2020. In contrast, cases among the wider population of Exeter rose steadily throughout the autumn. It is not possible to determine from this whether the arrival of students in Exeter had an impact on the rising levels of COVID-19 in the wider community, as infections were also increasing across the country during the autumn. Research into the transmission of COVID-19 at certain English universities is presented in How has coronavirus (COVID-19) spread among students in England?. The findings reflect the situation at individual institutions, and cannot be applied to the higher education sector as a whole.
sourcename: How has coronavirus (COVID-19) spread among students in England?

title: The percentage of people with antibodies against COVID-19 was highest in England and lowest in Scotland
subtitle: Estimated percentage of people testing positive for antibodies to COVID-19 from a blood sample, by 28-day periods, 28 April 2020 to 1 February 2021, UK nations
commentary: The percentage of people testing positive for COVID-19 antibodies increased across all four UK nations. In the 28 days up to 1 February 2021, an estimated 1 in 5 people in England, 1 in 7 people in Wales, 1 in 7 people in Northern Ireland and 1 in 9 people in Scotland would have tested positive for antibodies to COVID-19. The presence of antibodies suggests a person has previously had COVID-19, or has been vaccinated.
sourcename: Coronavirus (COVID-19) Infection Survey: antibody data for the UK

title: Over 40% of adults aged 80 years and over in England had antibodies against COVID-19
subtitle: Estimated percentage of people testing positive for antibodies to COVID-19 from a blood sample, by age, 5 January to 1 February 2021, UK nations
commentary: In England, adults aged 80 years and over had the highest antibody postivity rate at 40.9%. However, the true figure for this age group may be different since adults in care homes, who were prioritised for vaccination, are not included in this survey. The second highest antibody positivity rate was seen in those aged 16 to 24 years at 25.9%. The lowest antibody positivity rate was seen in those aged 70 to 74 years at 10.5%. Adults aged 80 years and over in Wales and Scotland had antibody positivity rates of 12.7%, and 11.6% respectively, with 9.1% for those aged 70 and over in Northern Ireland.
sourcename: Coronavirus (COVID-19) Infection Survey: antibody data for the UK

title: Antibody positivity was above the national average in London, the North West, the West Midlands and Yorkshire and The Humber
subtitle: Estimated percentage of people testing positive for antibodies to COVID-19 from a blood sample, by region, 5 January to 1 February 2021, England
commentary: Antibody positivity increased in all English regions in the 28 days to 1 February 2021, compared to the previous 28 day period to 4 January 2021. There is substantial variation in the percentage testing positive for COVID-19 antibodies across English regions. London had the highest antibody positivity rate at 24.8%, while the lowest antibody positivity rate was in the South West, at 11.6%. The south and the East of England had the lowest antibody positivity rates.
sourcename: Coronavirus (COVID-19) Infection Survey: antibody data for the UK

title: Around half (49%) of Black or Black British adults reported they would be likely to have the vaccine
subtitle: Great Britain, 10 December 2020 to 10 January 2021
commentary: Around half (49%) of individuals from the "Black or Black British" ethnic group reported that they would be very or fairly likely to have the COVID-19 vaccine if offered it. This is a lower proportion than in the "White" (85%), "Mixed" (80%) and "Asian or Asian British" (72%) ethnic groups. Of those in the "other" ethnic group, 65% reported that they would be very or fairly likely to have the vaccine.
sourcename: Coronavirus and the social impacts on Great Britain
